layers.name: Requests & workloads
layers.invariant: A request supplies inputs, a desired output, and a quality/latency budget.
layers.observe: Prompt construction → token spans → requests and dependencies → output acceptance.
layers.examples: Tokenizers, multimodal inputs, retrieval, agent loops, prompt layout, test-time search, speculative decoding.
layers.benefit: Less repeated input or fewer expensive target-model steps.
layers.cost: Extra retrieval/draft work, acceptance overhead, and changed workload or output quality.
layers.fit: Good for token accounting and request traces; weak for general task quality.

layers.name: Model & learned computation
layers.invariant: Parameters and architecture transform inputs and state into output scores.
layers.observe: Layer graph, routing, activations, logits, and the training provenance of weights.
layers.examples: New checkpoints, dense versus MoE, depth/width, FFNs, adapters and their inference effects.
layers.benefit: Different capacity, specialization, or work per token.
layers.cost: Training requirements, routing imbalance, quality shifts, and parameter storage.
layers.fit: Inspectable arithmetic; very weak predictor of large-model capabilities.

layers.name: Token mixing & sequence state
layers.invariant: A token reads or updates a representation of preceding context.
layers.observe: Queries, keys, values, masks, routing, recurrent state, writes, reads, and forgetting.
layers.examples: MHA, GQA, MLA, sparse/sliding attention, Kimi Delta Attention, recurrent and hybrid designs.
layers.benefit: Reduced state or work; changed control over information retention.
layers.cost: Information bottlenecks, retrieval errors, and different training needs.
layers.fit: Good for state-update mechanics; limited for learned retrieval and long-context quality.

layers.name: Numerical representation
layers.invariant: Every value has a representation and every operation has an arithmetic policy.
layers.observe: Storage/compute/accumulation dtype, scales, rounding, clipping, and propagated error.
layers.examples: Weight/activation/KV quantization, mixed precision, sparsity encodings, calibration.
layers.benefit: Fewer stored or transferred bytes and potentially cheaper arithmetic.
layers.cost: Approximation error, metadata, conversions, and hardware-dependent support.
layers.fit: Good for exact local error; weak for production accuracy or throughput predictions.

layers.name: Execution framework & compiler
layers.invariant: A declared model must become an executable graph with concrete layouts and lifetimes.
layers.observe: Graph lowering, dispatch, fusion, allocations, synchronization, and graph breaks.
layers.examples: Model frameworks, graph compilers, runtime backends, execution graphs, operator lowering.
layers.benefit: Less dispatch and intermediate materialization; better scheduling.
layers.cost: Compilation, dynamic-shape constraints, unsupported operators, and debugging complexity.
layers.fit: Low transfer from a tiny interpreter. Real framework traces and representative shapes are required.

layers.name: Operators & kernels
layers.invariant: Operators consume operands, execute arithmetic, and move data through memory.
layers.observe: Tiles, reads/writes, intermediate storage, reductions, and launch boundaries.
layers.examples: Fused attention, GEMM variants, chunkwise recurrence, communication/computation overlap.
layers.benefit: Less memory traffic and better utilization.
layers.cost: Shape constraints, numerical differences, implementation complexity, and hardware specialization.
layers.fit: Useful operation/byte models; tiny Python timings say little about accelerator performance.

layers.name: State storage & reuse
layers.invariant: Reused state must match the computation, input prefix, and configuration that produced it.
layers.observe: Cache keys, hits/misses, blocks, reference counts, invalidation, eviction, and transfers.
layers.examples: KV allocation, exact prefix caching, paging, offload, state compression, cache-aware prompt layout.
layers.benefit: Avoided recomputation and more effective memory use.
layers.cost: Lookup/transfer/storage work, fragmentation, stale-state risks, and eviction pressure.
layers.fit: Good for exact reuse semantics and accounting; hit rate depends on real workloads.

layers.name: Serving & scheduling
layers.invariant: Finite capacity must be shared among requests over time.
layers.observe: Arrivals, queues, batches, admission, preemption, cancellation, and token timelines.
layers.examples: Continuous batching, chunked prefill, cache-aware scheduling, routing, admission control.
layers.benefit: Higher utilization or improved latency under a stated objective.
layers.cost: Queueing, interference, fairness tradeoffs, and tail latency.
layers.fit: Useful event simulation; production conclusions require representative arrivals and service times.

layers.name: Placement & distributed topology
layers.invariant: Work and state are placed on resources and dependencies cross communication links.
layers.observe: Worker placement, shards, collectives, transfers, overlap, and handoff critical paths.
layers.examples: Prefill/decode disaggregation, tensor/pipeline/expert/context parallelism, multi-node routing.
layers.benefit: Phase specialization, capacity scaling, or isolation.
layers.cost: Communication, state handoff, idle resources, and coordination.
layers.fit: Useful dependency and transfer models; real network contention and scaling need external evidence.

layers.name: Hardware, memory & physical resources
layers.invariant: Compute, capacity, bandwidth, latency, power, and cooling are finite resources.
layers.observe: Operations, bytes by tier/link, residency, utilization, energy assumptions, and cost.
layers.examples: Accelerators, interconnects, HBM/DRAM/SSD and proposed memory tiers, near-memory compute, power/cooling changes.
layers.benefit: More capacity, faster arithmetic or transfer, or lower energy per useful result.
layers.cost: Bottleneck shifts, purchase/operating costs, endurance, and workload dependence.
layers.fit: Explicit resource models only unless measured on the actual system; no vendor-performance inference.

innovations.name: Kimi Delta Attention (KDA)
innovations.summary: Inspect a two-channel delta-rule memory update with channel-wise forgetting. This is a recurrence demonstrator, not a trained Kimi model.
innovations.mechanism: Decay the state by channel, read the current key, write a correction toward its value, then read with the query.
innovations.benefit: The recurrent state has fixed size with respect to sequence length.
innovations.cost: Finite-state compression changes what can be retrieved. It is not a token-addressable KV history.
innovations.limit: Hand-selected vectors and gates; no learned projections, short convolution, output gating, hybrid layers, or optimized chunkwise kernel. No accuracy or speed claim.
innovations.question: Which coordinates survive a gate change, and how does an interfering write affect a later read?

innovations.name: Exact prefix caching
innovations.summary: Follow reuse of state for an identical prefix across requests.
innovations.mechanism: Compare prefix and model/config identities; reuse matching state and compute the remaining tokens.
innovations.benefit: Avoid repeated prefix computation when valid state is available.
innovations.cost: State consumes capacity; lookups, transfers, and eviction can erase the gain.
innovations.limit: Implemented scope: exact whole-prefix reuse with LRU retention, bounded KV reservations, and optional CUDA/pinned-DRAM transfers. No partial-prefix paging, batching, calibrated accelerator timing, or fleet savings claim.
innovations.question: When do lookup and transfer cost exceed avoided prefill work?

innovations.name: Prefill/decode disaggregation
innovations.summary: Follow a request from a prefill worker through state transfer to a decode worker.
innovations.mechanism: Place prompt processing and token generation on separate resources and transfer the required state.
innovations.benefit: Explore independent resource allocation and phase interference.
innovations.cost: Handoff bytes, network delay, queueing, and unused capacity can dominate.
innovations.limit: An event/cost model must state bandwidth, latency, arrivals, and service-time assumptions; it is not a cluster benchmark.
innovations.question: At what prompt size, arrival rate, and link cost does separation help the chosen latency objective?

innovations.name: Speculative decoding
innovations.summary: Propose candidate tokens, verify with a target, and expose accepted output and discarded work.
innovations.mechanism: Separate draft proposals, target verification, commitment, and client delivery.
innovations.benefit: Potentially amortize target execution over several accepted output tokens.
innovations.cost: Draft and verification work, rejected suffixes, state management, and resource contention.
innovations.limit: Greedy equivalence and distribution-preserving sampling are separate claims. Tiny timings and acceptance rates do not establish production speedup.
innovations.question: What happens when the first candidate is rejected, every candidate is accepted, or draft overhead exceeds saved target work?

sources.title: Fast Inference from Transformers via Speculative Decoding, ICML 2023
